***Ghost in the Shell*** ([Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language): 攻殻機動隊, [Hepburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepburn_romanization): *Kōkaku Kidōtai*; lit. 'Mobile Armored Riot Police') is a [Japanese cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_cyberpunk) [manga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manga) series written and illustrated by [Masamune Shirow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masamune_Shirow). It was first serialized in [Kodansha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodansha)'s [*seinen* manga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seinen_manga) magazine [*Young Magazine*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weekly_Young_Magazine) *Zōkan Kaizokuban* from 1989 to 1990, and was then compiled in a single [*tankōbon*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tank%C5%8Dbon) volume. Shirow produced two [sequels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequels): *Ghost in the Shell 1.5: Human-Error Processor* and *Ghost in the Shell 2: Man-Machine Interface*. Set in the mid-21st-century, the manga tells the story of the fictional counter-[cyberterrorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberterrorist) organization [Public Security Section 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Security_Section_9), led by protagonist Major [Motoko Kusanagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motoko_Kusanagi).

The manga contain Shirow's thoughts on design and philosophy, including sociological issues, the consequences of technological advances and themes on the nature of consciousness and identity. Several artbooks have been released to detail the concept art and the world of *Ghost in the Shell*.

All three volumes have received mainly positive reviews. The manga spawned a media franchise [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell), starting with the 1995 anime feature film [*Ghost in the Shell*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(1995_film\)). Starting in 2019, a collaborative manga by [Junichi Fujisaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junichi_Fujisaku) (writer) and Yuki Yoshimoto (illustrator), titled *Ghost in the Shell: The Human Algorithm*, was made as the sequel to *GiTS 1.5*.

**Synopsis**

**Setting**

Primarily set in the mid-twenty-first century in the fictional Japanese city of Niihama, Niihama Prefecture,[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-2)[\[Note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-3) otherwise known as New Port City,[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-4) the manga and the many [anime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anime) adaptations follow the members of [Public Security Section 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Security_Section_9), a special-operations task-force made up of former military officers and police detectives. Political intrigue and counter-terrorism operations are standard fare for Section 9, but the various actions of corrupt officials, companies, and cyber-criminals in each scenario are unique and require the diverse skills of Section 9's staff to prevent a series of incidents from escalating.

In this [cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk) iteration of a possible future, computer technology has advanced to the point that many members of the public possess cyberbrains, technology that allows them to interface their biological brain with various networks. The level of cyberization varies from simple minimal interfaces to almost complete replacement of the brain with cybernetic parts, in cases of severe trauma. This can also be combined with various levels of [prostheses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostheses), with a fully prosthetic body enabling a person to become a [cyborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyborg). The heroine of *Ghost in the Shell*, Major [Motoko Kusanagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motoko_Kusanagi), is such a cyborg, having had a terrible accident befall her as a child that ultimately required that she use a full-body prosthesis to house her cyberbrain. This high level of cyberization, however, opens the brain up to attacks from highly skilled [hackers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacker_\(computer_security\)), with the most dangerous being those who will hack a person to bend to their whims.

**Story**

*Main article: [List of](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ghost_in_the_Shell_characters)* [Ghost in the Shell *characters*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ghost_in_the_Shell_characters)

*Ghost in the Shell*[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-5) begins in 2029, and features Section 9, led by Chief [Daisuke Aramaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daisuke_Aramaki) and Major [Motoko Kusanagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motoko_Kusanagi), as they investigate the Puppeteer, a cyber-criminal wanted for committing a large number of crimes by proxy through "ghost hacking" humans with cyberbrains. As the investigation continues, Section 9 discovers that the Puppet Master is actually an advanced [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence) created by a department of the Japanese government, taking up residence in a robot body. After destroying the latest host of the Puppeteer, Section 9 believes all is well, until the Major discovers the Puppet Master in her own mind. After hearing the Puppeteer's wishes to reach its next step in evolution, Kusanagi allows it to become one with her own ghost.

In *Ghost in the Shell 1.5: Human-Error Processor*[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-6) the Major leaves Section 9 to work as a private contractor, with the remaining members of the unit, [Batou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batou), [Togusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Togusa), Ishikawa, Saito, Paz, Borma and Azuma, continuing their work as covert operatives, occasionally meeting up with the Major only in the chapter "Drive Slave".

*Ghost in the Shell 2: Man-Machine Interface*[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-7) This story is set four years and five months after Motoko Kusanagi fused with a sentient life form and left Public Security Section 9\. The fused being of Motoko and the Puppeteer have been traveling the sea of the Net, merging with other ghosts and creating isotopes. Among them, Motoko Aramaki, the head of the Investigative Division at Poseidon Industrial, began investigating an incident involving an attack on a pig clone organ cultivation facility owned by its subsidiary, Meditech. As she delved into the investigation, she found herself making contact with other isotopes when infiltrating Motoko Kusanagi in a secretive club known as the "Sleeping Universe," a facility used for the transfer of consciousness.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-8)

**Production**

**Creation and development**

While writing the manga, Masamune Shirow struggled to make it neither too complex nor too simple.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-MS-interview-9) Two official names exist for the works, the first is *Kōkaku Kidōtai* (攻殻機動隊, officially "*Armored Shell*"; literally "*Mobile Armored Riot Police*") and the second is "*Ghost in the Shell*". Masamune Shirow originally wanted to use the name "*Ghost in the Shell*" for the publication, as an homage to [Arthur Koestler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Koestler)'s [*The Ghost in the Machine*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ghost_in_the_Machine), from which he drew inspiration.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-SAC-Log1-10) Kōichi Yuri, First Coordinator at *Young Magazine*, requested a "more flashy" name and Shirow came up with *Kōkaku Kidōtai* (攻殻機動隊, Shell Squad). Shirow requested that "Ghost in the Shell" be included on the title even if it was in small print. Yuri believes that *Kōkaku Kidōtai* is the mainstream title while "Ghost in the Shell" is the theme. While most Japanese publications use both names, the original publication in *Young Magazine* used *Kōkaku Kidōtai*.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-SAC-Log1-10)

When developing *Ghost in the Shell 2: Man-Machine Interface*, Shirow initially wanted to use a new title by changing the last [kanji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanji) character meaning "military unit" (隊, *tai*), to the homophonic kanji for "body" (体, *tai*) so that it would literally translate "Mobile Unit Body Entity" (攻殻機動体, *Kōkaku Kidōtai*), but eventually he decided not to do so.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Gits2_notes-11) The production of *Ghost in the Shell 2: Man-Machine Interface* manga was done digitally, which was difficult for Shirow because of troubles including a hard disk failure which resulted in the loss of 16 gigabytes of data, USB hardware troubles and reading manuals related to new application upgrades. Shirow considers the manga a completely different kind of work and not a true sequel of *Ghost in the Shell*. The original manga revolved around Public Security Section 9 and *Ghost in the Shell 2: Man-Machine Interface* follows what happens to the Major after she merges with the Puppeteer. Shirow drew the color pages on computer, in which he states was difficult to do due to technical issues with his computer. In the "short-cut" version of the manga, Masamune Shirow made the color darker and softer, but used more contrasting colors in the "standard" version.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-MS-interview-2-12) In the Japanese "Short-cut" version, further changes can be found, most notably an increase in nudity and explicit scenes.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-Comparisons-13)\[[*better source needed*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:NOTRS)\]

**Design and philosophy**

Shirow's thoughts and work on *Ghost in the Shell* contain numerous footnotes and detailed explanations about scenes to give readers an understanding of the sociological differences or technological advances and philosophical discussion of the material. Examples include concepts like the future of hacking techniques, in which a cyberbrain can be hacked to copy information without being detected. Shirow explains instances of spirit channeling in cyborgs with [kiko energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qigong). Shirow even wrote that this phenomenon may be related to the "hearing voices" in individuals that suffer from mental disabilities like [schizophrenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schizophrenia). This belief is represented in Motoko's reasons for head hunting Togusa for Section 9\.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-dh1-14) Shirow also notes that he believes these channelers do not speak with a human-like god, but instead tap into a phase of the universe which synchronizes with the channeler's functions. Other philosophical stances are represented such as Shirow's personal beliefs regarding [death sentences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_sentence) and crime and punishment.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-dh1-14)

Shirow explains numerous facets of the daily life throughout his notes in *Ghost in the Shell*. Cyborgs are shown consuming food, but Shirow noted that early in the development would have been pills or paste substance that would have both psychological and physical functions. The Fuchikoma [robots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robot) also must consume in a sense, requiring replenishment of fluid for their [neurochips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurochip) every two months, but Fuchikoma are not entirely bio-robots. Shirow discussed in his notes how the family of Yano received notification of his death and what would be disclosed, but also notes strategic use and premature notifications exist for various purposes. The advancement of technology in Shirow's vision of the future is rapid, but the advancements are at least partially related to then-current technology. The concepts of a 3-D viewing room were based on "crude" golf simulator technology.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-dh1-14)

Other personal beliefs of Shirow are represented in the scenes and author's commentary, such as [metaphysics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaphysics), religious references, and other philosophical stances that enter a range of topics including his thoughts on a rotating universe.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-dh1-14)

**Censorship**

The removal of a two-page lesbian sex scene in [Studio Proteus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Proteus)'s localization of *Ghost in the Shell* was not well received, with readers reacting negatively to the removal of the previously uncensored content that was included in the original [Dark Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Horse_Comics) release. [Toren Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toren_Smith) commented on Studio Proteus's actions claiming that requirement of the "mature readers only" would translate into a 40% loss in sales and likely have caused the immediate cancellation of the series. Shirow, who grew tired of "taking flak" over the pages, opted to remove them and reworked the previous page as necessary.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Toren-15)

The sequel volume *Ghost in the Shell 2: Man-Machine Interface* also featured explicit scenes and an increase in nudity in the "Short-cut" version in Japan.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-Comparisons2-16)\[[*better source needed*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:NOTRS)\]

**Publication**

*Ghost in the Shell* ran in the [Kodansha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodansha)'s manga anthology [*Young Magazine Kaizokuban*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weekly_Young_Magazine) from the April 1989 to the November 1990 issues,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-17)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-PR-times-18)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Natalie1-19) and was released in [*tankōbon*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tank%C5%8Dbon) format on October 2, 1991\.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS-KC-20) Dark Horse initially published it in English monthly into eight comic issues from March 1, 1995, to October 1, 1995, with the translation of [Studio Proteus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Proteus).[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS-1/8-21)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS-8/8-22) It was collected into a [trade paperback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_paperback_\(comics\)) volume on December 1, 1995\.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS-1E-23) An uncensored version was released by [Dark Horse Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Horse_Comics) on October 6, 2004\.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS1-2E-24) The censored version was later republished by [Kodansha Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodansha_Comics) in 2009 and 2017\.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS1-US-KC-25)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Tumblr-26)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Hardcover-27)

Masamune Shirow penned the sequel *Ghost in the Shell 2: Man-Machine Interface* and ran in [*Weekly Young Magazine*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weekly_Young_Magazine) in 1997\. The chapters were collected into a [hardcover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardcover) volume along with its predecessor in a limited-edition box set titled *Kōkaku Kidōtai Solid Box*[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-28) on December 1, 2000\. The box set also contained a booklet titled *ManMachine Interface Inactive Module*, a poster, and a Fuchikoma robot action figure.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-solidbox-KC-29) The *Solid Box* version added over 140 pages of new content. The *tankōbon* version was released on June 26, 2001, and included more changes, such as 24 color pages and over 20 large modifications to existing pages.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-soft-KC-30) The manga was then distributed in English by Dark Horse Comics in 11 comic issues from January 29, 2003, to December 31, 2003\.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-1/11-31)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-11/11-32) Masamune Shirow manually redrew the manga for the English version so that it could be read from left to right.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-ICV2-33) It was collected into a single volume in trade paperback on January 12, 2005\.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-TPB-34) The manga was republished by Kodansha Comics on August 10, 2010\.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-US-KC-35)

Four chapters from the sequel's run that were published from 1991 to 1996 and not released in *tankōbon* format in previous releases were later collected into a single volume titled *Ghost in the Shell 1.5: Human-Error Processor*. The manga was published on July 17, 2003, by Kodansha.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS1.5-KC-36) It included a booklet and a CD-ROM featuring the full stories, adding music to the manga scenes, and a screen saver.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS1.5-CD-37) Dark Horse Comics announced an English version at the 2005 [San Diego Comic-Con](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_Comic-Con_International).[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-DH-Comic-Con-38) The four chapters were each split into two, and released as eight individual comic issues from November 1, 2006, to June 6, 2007, and was the first of the *Ghost in the Shell* manga released in the United States to read right-to-left.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS1.5-1/8-39)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS1.5-8/8-40) Dark Horse Comics later released it in a single trade paperback volume on October 10, 2007\.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS1.5-TPB-41) The manga was later republished by Kodansha Comics on September 25, 2012\.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS1.5-US-KC-42)

A box set containing the three manga volumes in hardcover and a lithograph by Masamune Shirow was released by Kodansha Comics on December 19, 2017, titled *The Ghost in the Shell Deluxe Complete Box Set*.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-HC-boxset-43) Kodansha Comics also compiled the three manga as a single hardcover volume with a new cover art by Masamune Shirow on January 10, 2023, titled *The Ghost in the Shell: Fully Compiled*.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Fully-Compiled-HC-44)

A sequel to *1.5* by [Junichi Fujisaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junichi_Fujisaku) and Yuki Yoshimoto, titled *Ghost in the Shell: The Human Algorithm*, started in Kodansha's *Comic Days* digital platform on September 16, 2019; the manga was also published in *Monthly Young Magazine* from September 20, 2019, to November 18, 2021\.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS:HA-announcement-45)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-ANN-announcement-46)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Natalie-THA-Start-47)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS:HA-P2-announcement-48) The series is set to end with its eighth volume in 2025\.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GIST:HA-END-49) In North America, it is published under Kodansha Comics.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-NA-release-50)

|  "01 Prologue" "02 Super Spartan – 10.4.2029" "03 Junk Jungle – 27.7.2029" "04 Megatech Machine 1 – Revolt of the Robots" "05 Megatech Machine 2 – The Making of a Cyborg" "06 Robot Rondo – 1.10.2029" "07 Phantom Fund – 24.12.2029" "08 Dumb Barter – 2.5.2030" "09 Bye Bye Clay – 15.7.2030" "10 Brain Drain – 9.9.2030" "11 Ghost Coast – 18.9.2030"  |  |  |  |
| In 2029 [Public Security Section 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Security_Section_9) led by Major [Motoko Kusanagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motoko_Kusanagi) hunts down the [Puppet Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppet_Master_\(Ghost_in_the_Shell\)), a cyber-criminal wanted for committing a large number of crimes by proxy through "ghost hacking" humans with cyberbrains. The investigation soon discovers that the Puppet Master is actually an advanced artificial intelligence project developed by Section 6, the Treaty Bureau of the [Ministry of Foreign Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Foreign_Affairs_\(Japan\)). After subduing the Puppet Master's robot host and destroying it, they believe the Puppet Master is gone, but the Major believes otherwise, and is proven right when she discovers the Puppet Master in her own cyberbrain. The Puppet Master wishes to seek its next step in evolution, and Kusanagi allows it to merge with her ghost. |  |  |  |
| 1.5 | *Ghost in the Shell 1.5: Human-Error Processor Kōkaku Kidōtai Itten Go Hyūman Erā Purosessā* (攻殻機動隊1.5 HUMAN-ERROR PROCESSER) | July 23, 2003[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS1.5-KC-36) [978-4-06-350406-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-4-06-350406-4) | October 10, 2007[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS1.5-TPB-41) [978-1-59307-815-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-1-59307-815-7) |
|  "Fat Cat" 01 and 02 "Drive Slave" 01 and 02 "Mines of Mind" 01 and 02 "Lost Past"  |  |  |  |
| This volume chronicles four cases Section 9 investigates between Volume 1 and 2\. In "Fat Cat", the team investigates a man's recent strange activities at the behest of his daughter, one of Chief [Daisuke Aramaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daisuke_Aramaki)'s friends. In "Drive Slave", Section 9 protects a key witness in a court case from various cyborg assassins sent to kill him, while Major Kusanagi arrives, having been sent to capture the man responsible for the assassins. The story "Mines of the Mind" features [Batou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batou) and [Togusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Togusa) investigating a series of murders, with all the victims marked with the same tattoo. In "Lost Past", the investigation into a kidnapping gone wrong has Section 9 suspecting that Section 6 hired a sniper to make it go wrong in the first place. |  |  |  |
| 2 | *Ghost in the Shell 2: Man-Machine Interface Kōkaku Kidōtai Ni Manmashīn Intāfēsu* (攻殻機動隊2 MANMACHINE INTERFACE) | June 26, 2001[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-soft-KC-30) [4-06-336310-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/4-06-336310-4) | January 12, 2005[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-TPB-34) [1-59307-204-X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/1-59307-204-X) |
|  "01 Prologue 2035.03.06.AM05:05" "02 Underwater 2035.03.06.AM05:45" "03 Circuit Weapon 2035.03.06.PM01:12" "04 Fly by Orbit 2035.03.06.PM01:12" "05 Mold of Life 2035.03.06.PM01:54" "06 Epilogue 2035.03.06.05:35AM"  |  |  |  |
| This story is set four years and five months after Motoko Kusanagi fused with a sentient life form and left Public Security Section 9\. The fused being of Motoko and the Puppeteer have been traveling the sea of the Net, merging with other ghosts and creating isotopes. Among them, Motoko Aramaki, the head of the Investigative Division at Poseidon Industrial, began investigating an incident involving an attack on a pig clone organ cultivation facility owned by its subsidiary, Meditech. As she delved into the investigation, she found herself making contact with other isotopes when infiltrating Motoko Kusanagi in a secretive club known as the "Sleeping Universe," a facility used for the transfer of consciousness. |  |  |  |

**Related media**

*Main article: [Ghost in the Shell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell)*

A number of artbooks detailing the concept art and world of *Ghost in the Shell* have been released. A box set titled *Kōkaku Kidōtai Cyberdelics*[\[g\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-51) was released on July 8, 1997\. The box set contains a collection of posters illustrated by Masamune Shirow, a booklet and a puzzle.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Cyberdelics-52) A guidebook titled *The Ghost in the Shell: Mechanical Analysis Reader*[\[h\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-53) was published by Kodansha and released on January 16, 1998\.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Mechanical_Analysis_Reader-54) An art book titled *The Ghost in the Shell: Fuchikoma Papercraft*[\[i\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-55) was released by Kodansha on July 24, 2000\. The book contains several different artwork and paper cut out figures of the Fuchikoma.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Fuchikoma_Papercraft-56)

The [*Ghost in the Shell* video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(video_game\)) was developed by Exact and released for the [PlayStation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_\(console\)) on July 17, 1997, in Japan by [Sony Computer Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Computer_Entertainment).[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Video_game-57) It is a [third-person shooter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third-person_shooter) featuring an original storyline where the character plays a rookie member of Section 9\.

A [VR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_reality) [Noh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noh) stage play adaptation was presented in [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo)'s [Setagaya Public Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Setagaya_Public_Theatre&action=edit&redlink=1) \[[ja](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%B8%96%E7%94%B0%E8%B0%B7%E3%83%91%E3%83%96%E3%83%AA%E3%83%83%E3%82%AF%E3%82%B7%E3%82%A2%E3%82%BF%E3%83%BC)\] on August 22 and 23, 2020,[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-58) and has since also been performed in [Fukuoka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka) and [Sapporo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapporo).[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-59)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-60)

**Film and television**

Animation studio [Production I.G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Production_I.G) has produced several different anime adaptations of *Ghost in the Shell*, starting with the 1995 film [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(1995_film\)), telling the story of Section 9's investigation of the [Puppet Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppet_Master_\(Ghost_in_the_Shell\)). The film was followed by a sequel titled [*Ghost in the Shell 2: Innocence*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_2:_Innocence), released in 2004\.

Meanwhile, a television series release began in 2002 under the title [*Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell:_Stand_Alone_Complex), telling an alternate story from the manga and first film, featuring Section 9's investigations of government corruption in the [Laughing Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laughing_Man_\(Ghost_in_the_Shell\)) and [Individual Eleven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual_Eleven) incidents. The series ran for two seasons of 26 episodes each, with the second season titled *Ghost in the Shell: S.A.C. 2nd GIG*. In 2006 a sequel film to the S.A.C. series was produced as [*Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex \- Solid State Society*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell:_Stand_Alone_Complex_-_Solid_State_Society). A Netflix continuation, [*Ghost in the Shell: SAC\_2045*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell:_SAC_2045), ran for two seasons of twelve episodes each in 2020 and 2022\.

2013 saw the start of the [*Ghost in the Shell: Arise*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell:_Arise) [OVA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Original_video_animation) series, set before the events of the original manga and consisting of four parts released through mid-2014. The series was recompiled in early 2015 as a television series titled [*Ghost in the Shell: Arise – Alternative Architecture*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell:_Arise#Anime), airing with an additional two episodes (one part).[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-Arise-TV-61) An animated feature film produced by most of the *Arise* staff, titled [*Ghost in the Shell: The New Movie*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell:_The_New_Movie), was released on June 20, 2015\.

A [live-action American-produced adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(2017_film\)) starring [Scarlett Johansson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarlett_Johansson) as The Major was released in the United States on March 31, 2017, by [Paramount Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Pictures).[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-62)

**Reception**

*Ghost in the Shell* has received mainly positive reviews. [*Publishers Weekly*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers_Weekly) praised the manga for its artwork: "Masamune's b\&w drawings are dynamic and beautifully gestural; he vividly renders the awesome urban landscape of a futuristic, supertechnological Japan."[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-63) Leroy Douresseaux of the website ComicBookBin gave the manga an "A" stating: "It is visually potent and often inscrutable, but its sense of wonder and exploration makes its ideas still seem fresh two decades after its debut."[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-64) Peter Gutiérrez of the website Graphic Novel Reporter praised the manga, writing: "In short, *Ghost in the Shell* is hard sci-fi of the best possible sort: the type that's so full of both undiluted artfulness and philosophy that it's arguably a must-read even for those who don't usually take to the genre."[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-65) Greg McElhatton of Read About Comics praised the artwork, however criticized the manga for its story pacing and collection of short adventures stating, "I'm glad I got to experience Shirow's artistic view of the future and am a little interested in the idea of his *Intron Depot* art books, but on the whole *Ghost in the Shell* was a massive shell game: flashy and fascinating from a glance, but ultimately empty when you decide to dive in."[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-66)

*Ghost in the Shell 2: Man-Machine Interface* has sold over 100,000 copies from its initial printing in Japan.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-GITS2-interview-67) [Diamond Comic Distributors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond_Comic_Distributors) ranked the manga \#7 in its Top Performing Manga list of 2005\.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-68) Mike Crandol of [*Anime News Network*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anime_News_Network) criticized the manga for being too complex and overwhelming stating it is "too technical for its own good" but praised the new artwork, stating that Shirow's "canny drawing skills are supplemented by an innovative use of [CGI graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_animation) that represent the series' boldest artistic endeavor."[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-69) *Publishers Weekly* praised the artwork as "the color and b\&w graphics are stunning, brilliantly evoking the nonvisual world of data transmission" but stated that the story can be confusing.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-70)

*Ghost in the Shell 1.5: Human-Error Processor* was ranked \#10 in [*The New York Times*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times) Manga Best Seller List on October 19, 2012\.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-71) Scott Green of [*Ain't It Cool News*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ain%27t_It_Cool_News) praised the manga for its footnotes that "alone are worth the price of admission. The degree to which he apparently takes every aspect seriously and the amount of information he'd like to convey verges on a disorder."[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_in_the_Shell_\(manga\)#cite_note-72)

*  The real world [Niihama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niihama,_Ehime) is located in [Ehime Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ehime_Prefecture), and its name is written differently in Japanese.

*  攻殻機動隊 THE GHOST IN THE SHELL, *Kōkaku Kidōtai Za Gōsuto in za Sheru*; lit. 'Mobile Armored Riot Police: The Ghost in the Shell'  
*  攻殻機動隊1.5 HUMAN-ERROR PROCESSER, *Kōkaku Kidōtai Itten Go Hyūman Erā Purosessā*; lit. 'Mobile Armored Riot Police: Human-Error Processer \[[*sic*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic)\]'  
*  攻殻機動隊2 MANMACHINE INTERFACE, *Kōkaku Kidōtai Ni Manmashīn Intāfēsu*; lit. 'Mobile Armored Riot Police: Manmachine \[[*sic*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic)\] Interface'  
*  攻殻機動隊SOLID BOX  
*  攻殻機動隊Cyberdelics  
*  攻殻機動隊メカニカル解析読本, *Kōkaku Kidōtai Mekanikaru Kaiseki Dokuhon*  
*  攻殻機動隊フチコマ立体図鑑, *Kōkaku Kidōtai fuchikoma Rittai Zukan*
